outline.description: Sets out the parties, the premium-finance arrangements, the challenged cancellation process, and how the case reached the Fifth Circuit on cross-motions for summary judgment focused on statutory compliance.
subtopics: Parties: Plaintiffs Williams, Wright (former insureds), Jenkins (third-party claimant); Defendants GoAuto Insurance and APAC (premium finance company)
Premium-finance structure: APAC pays full premium; insureds pay APAC in installments; APAC holds power of attorney to cancel upon default
Events: Nonpayment by insureds; APAC initiates cancellation; accident involving a third GoAuto insured and Jenkins
Claims: Ineffective cancellations under Louisiana statute; misrepresentation; breach of good faith and fair dealing

Procedural path: State court filing; removal to M.D. La.; cross-motions for summary judgment limited to statutory compliance; district court grants GoAuto’s motion; dismissal with prejudice; appeal by Plaintiffs

outline.chapter_title: Louisiana Framework for Cancelling Financed Insurance Policies
outline.description: Explains the governing statute and the judicial requirement of strict adherence, setting the baseline against which GoAuto/APAC’s procedures are measured.
subtopics: Statutory source: La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)

How cancellation is requested: Premium finance company sends to insurer—by mail, private carrier, or email—a copy of the insured’s notice of cancellation plus a statement certifying four items (§ 9:3550(G)(3)(a)(i)–(iv))
Four certification elements: valid power of attorney; default not timely cured; notice to insured specifying date sent; notice to all interested third parties with names/addresses
Trigger for insurer action: Upon receipt of the notice and statement, insurer may proceed to cancel (§ 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i))
Judicial gloss: strict adherence required; any defect renders cancellation ineffective (Delatte; Eaglin; Britten)
Policy purposes of strict adherence: fix exact cancellation time/date; ensure minimum cure period (Britten)

outline.chapter_title: The Challenged Procedures and the Legal Questions Presented
outline.description: Details APAC/GoAuto’s actual workflow and distills the specific interpretive disputes: whether a signature is required to 'certify' and what constitutes insurer 'receipt' under the statute.
subtopics: APAC workflow: 10-day cure notice to insured; if unpaid by midnight day 10, automated email to GoAuto with notice of cancellation and certification; GoAuto’s system auto-cancels in early hours

Post-cancellation documentation: Later that morning, APAC employee applies signature stamp to printed documents; delivery to shared cabinet (pre-2017) or hand to GoAuto employee for 'received' stamp (post-2017)
Issue 1 – 'Certifying': Does § 9:3550 require a human signature or named employee on the certification before cancellation?
Issue 2 – 'Receipt': Does 'receipt' require physical possession by a GoAuto human before cancellation, or does electronic intake by GoAuto’s systems suffice?
Secondary district court rationale: 'Private carrier' theory for physical delivery (not reached on appeal)
Standard framing: strict statutory adherence; summary judgment focused on statutory compliance; Plaintiffs also sought partial summary judgment

outline.chapter_title: Court’s Analysis: Certification Without Signature and Electronic Receipt
outline.description: Presents the Fifth Circuit’s statutory interpretation, reliance on Louisiana appellate cases, and application to the APAC/GoAuto process.
subtopics: No signature requirement in statutory text: § 9:3550(G)(3)(a) speaks of the company 'certifying' but is silent on signatures

Louisiana case treatment: KMJ Services and Hodges paraphrase requirement as a 'statement certifying' and 'notice and statement' without mandating signatures; Benitez flagged lack of signature amid broader deficiencies but did not make it dispositive
Holding on certification: The company (APAC), not a named individual, can 'certify'; strict adherence does not permit courts to add a signature prerequisite
Defining 'receipt': Absence of statutory definition; reliance on Black’s Law Dictionary (12th ed. 2024) for 'receipt'/'receive' as taking possession/custody
Application to electronic systems: GoAuto’s web service 'listens' and, upon receiving APAC’s email/request, cancels automatically—this constitutes receipt before cancellation
No human involvement required pre-cancellation: Later signature stamping by APAC and physical filing do not undercut earlier electronic receipt
Declining the 'private carrier' rationale: District court’s alternative ground deemed unnecessary; Fifth Circuit affirms based on email receipt alone

outline.chapter_title: Disposition, Certification to State Court, and Practical Implications
outline.description: Concludes with the court’s refusal to certify questions to the Louisiana Supreme Court, the affirmance of summary judgment, and the case’s significance for insurers and premium finance companies.
subtopics: Certification to Louisiana Supreme Court denied: Novelty alone insufficient; court avoids overuse of certification (Jefferson v. Lead Industries Ass’n)
Disposition: District court correctly held procedures complied with § 9:3550; Plaintiffs’ motion for partial summary judgment properly denied; judgment AFFIRMED
Effect on ancillary claims: With valid cancellations, misrepresentation and good-faith claims against GoAuto fail and remain dismissed with prejudice

Key takeaways for practice: No signature or identified employee needed if the company’s certification covers statutory elements; electronic transmission and automated intake can satisfy 'receipt'; maintain records evidencing the four statutory certifications and timing
Boundary of strict adherence: Courts enforce statutory text strictly but will not add requirements not found in the statute
